prose.def: An adjective describing nard (an aromatic ointment) as genuine or pure, used only in the phrase 'pure nard.'
prose.article: In the New Testament this word appears just twice (Mark 14:3 and John 12:3), both times describing the expensive nard ointment poured on Jesus, and translators consistently take it to mean 'pure' or 'genuine.' Since it derives from πίστις (faith, trust), the underlying idea is 'trustworthy' or 'unadulterated,' which fits an unmixed, authentic perfume. The classical lexica record broader senses the New Testament never uses, including 'persuasive' (Plato) and 'faithful, trusty' of persons (Plutarch), so its everyday biblical sense is narrower than its full range.
prose.caution: This is a rare word with only 2 New Testament occurrences, and scholars have debated whether it comes from 'true/genuine' or from a word for liquid, leaving its precise meaning somewhat uncertain.

prose.def: A wanderer; describing stars that have strayed from their fixed paths.
prose.article: πλανήτης means "wanderer," built from the verb meaning to wander or go astray. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jude 13, where false teachers are compared to "wandering stars" that have left their appointed courses. The same word is the ordinary Greek term for a planet, and a third-century magical papyrus uses it exactly that way ("the five wandering stars"); in Jude, though, the imagery comes from the book of Enoch, picturing stars that have strayed from their orbits. Its only Septuagint appearance, in Hosea 9:17, renders a Hebrew word meaning "to wander."
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the measured sense rests on a single verse.

prose.def: The superlative of "much/many": the greatest amount, the most, or very many of something.
prose.article: πλεῖστος is the irregular superlative of πολύς ("much, many"), so it points to the largest quantity, the greatest degree, or—in the plural—very many. The papyri are especially telling here: Moulton-Milligan note the word is "generally elative," as in phrases like "with very many others," though genuine superlative uses also appear. It does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up only 4 times in the Septuagint, where it renders three different Hebrew words.

prose.def: To strike or hit something hard, often with the result of damage or harm.
prose.article: πλήσσω means to strike or smite, to hit with force. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Revelation 8:12), where it describes a third of the sun, moon, and stars being struck; there it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word. In the Septuagint it occurs 22 times in 8 books, chiefly translating the Hebrew nakah (to strike), and the everyday papyri use it vividly for real-world violence—one document complains of being struck "with her own hands," another reports a whole body "battered."

prose.def: A boat, originally meaning a small boat but in practice used for any ordinary vessel.
prose.article: πλοιάριον is technically a diminutive of πλοῖον ("ship"), so it literally means "little boat," but in actual use it is hardly distinguishable from the regular word for a boat. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "boat" in every case where it gets its own English word (3 of 6 occurrences in the Byzantine NT). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this overlap: one document interchanges πλοιάριον with the ordinary πλοῖον, showing the "small" sense had largely faded in common speech.

prose.def: A watercraft used for fishing, travel, or transport, ranging from a small fishing boat to a larger seagoing ship.
prose.article: πλοῖον covers any kind of vessel that floats and carries people or cargo. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 66 times, rendered "boat" in 65% of cases and "ship" in 30%, the smaller-versus-larger choice depending mostly on context, like the fishing boats of the Gospels versus the seagoing ships of Acts and Revelation. Interestingly, this everyday Koine word came to absorb the role of the older word ναῦς ("ship"), which had nearly vanished from common speech, and the papyri even mention a papyrus boat seen in a dream sailing to Memphis. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew אֳנִיָּה ("ship") 23 of 31 times.

prose.def: Having great wealth or possessions; used of people who are rich, and figuratively of being abundantly supplied with something.

The two senses are really the same idea — sometimes the word stands alone as a noun meaning "a rich man" (as in the camel-through-a-needle's-eye sayings). In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew עָשִׁיר ("rich") 15 times, and the everyday Koine papyri show the same plain meaning — one even calls a young man a "handsome and rich stripling." The lexica also note a figurative use, "abounding in," applied to God being rich in mercy, though that nuance is not separated out in the measured data here.

prose.def: In a rich, abundant, or generous way — having or giving something in large measure.
prose.article: πλουσίως is an adverb meaning "richly" or "abundantly," formed from the adjective for "rich." It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, and translators render it as "richly" half the time (as in Colossians 3:16 and 1 Timothy 6:17), with the other occurrences describing something poured out abundantly or received generously. An inscription from the first century BC (OGIS 767) uses it to commend a man who did his duties toward others "generously, beyond his ability," showing the word's everyday sense of lavish, open-handed measure.
prose.caution: With only 4 occurrences, the apparent "senses" are really one meaning ("richly/abundantly") shaded by context, not genuinely distinct definitions.

receipts.how: The adverb modifies the dwelling of Christ's word in believers 'richly,' directly supporting the core definition of abundant, generous measure.

It appears only twice in the New Testament, once for each sense—Acts 2:2 describes the sound of a violent wind at Pentecost, while Acts 17:25 speaks of God giving everyone life and breath. The breath sense dominates in the Septuagint, where the word renders the Hebrew נְשָׁמָה 13 times, including God breathing life into the first human in Genesis 2:7, and an ancient sundial inscription uses πνοή for the blowing of the west wind.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, confidence is low, though the Septuagint and classical evidence agree on the same two senses.

prose.caution: Confidence is rated low: this word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

prose.def: An interrogative adverb asking from what place, source, origin, or cause something comes — "where from?" or "how?"
prose.article: πόθεν is a question word meaning "from where?" — asking about the place, origin, source, or cause of something. About two-thirds of its 28 New Testament uses (16×) are rendered "where," but it also stretches to mean "how" (3×), as when Jesus asks how David could call the Messiah "Lord" (Mark 12:37). In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew phrase meaning "from where" (17×), and everyday papyri use it the same way — one document has people "declaring the sources from which" they acquired property.

prose.def: To make, create, or produce something, or to do, perform, or carry out an action.
prose.article: ποιέω is one of the most common and flexible verbs in the New Testament, appearing 574 times and covering everything from making and creating to doing, performing, and carrying out. About 38% of the time it's rendered "made," while the rest splits among "what," "done," "doing," and "things," reflecting how broadly it stretches across both production and action. In the Septuagint it appears a staggering 2,817 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew עָשָׂה ("to do/make") over 2,200 times; everyday papyri also show the polite phrase "you will do well" used much like our "please" when making a request.
prose.caution: The verb is so broad that in 381 of 574 occurrences it carries no English word of its own, getting absorbed into surrounding phrasing.

prose.def: Something that has been made or crafted; a created work or product.
prose.article: ποίημα refers to anything that has been made — a product, fabrication, or finished work — and it comes straight from the verb ποιέω, "to make." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times pointing to what God has made: the created world in Romans 1:20 and believers themselves as God's handiwork in Ephesians 2:10. The Septuagint uses it far more often (29 times), most frequently translating the Hebrew מַעֲשֶׂה ("work, deed"), and an inscription from 218–217 BC even uses the plural for an artisan's own "pieces of work," showing it was everyday vocabulary for crafted things.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range here is very thin and rests largely on the broader Septuagint and papyri evidence.

prose.def: The act of doing or carrying something out; a performance or making.
prose.article: ποίησις means "a doing" or "a making" — the noun built from ποιέω, "to do/make." It appears just once in the New Testament, at James 1:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the phrase "intently" as part of describing someone who acts on what they hear; the classical lexica (Herodotus, Thucydides) and the Septuagint's seven uses lean toward the basic ideas of "making" and "doing." A nice everyday witness comes from an inscription (211/210 BC) about "the making of the image," and in Modern Greek the word has narrowed to mean "poetry."
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a measured rendering ("intently") that reflects a translation phrasing rather than the word's own "doing/making" core, the evidence here is thin.

prose.def: Someone who does or carries out something, especially one who actively obeys a law or message rather than just hearing it.
prose.article: ποιητής comes from the verb ποιέω ("to do, make") and means a person who acts on something. In the New Testament it appears 6 times, regularly in phrases like "doer of the law" or "doer of the word" (James and Romans), where it stresses carrying something out rather than merely listening. Interestingly, in everyday Greek the same word commonly meant "poet" or "maker" — papyri and inscriptions call Homer "the divine poet" using this exact term, and Acts 17:28 uses it that way too.
prose.caution: With only 6 occurrences and the measured rendering folding it into surrounding phrasing almost every time, the English wording varies by context.

prose.def: Of many kinds or sorts; varied or diverse in character, originally referring to something many-colored or variegated.
prose.article: ποικίλος describes something that comes in many kinds or varieties, and in the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "various" or "kinds" in nearly every case, including the recurring use for people sick with "various diseases" (Matthew 4:24, Luke 4:40). The original concrete sense was "many-colored" or "variegated," which still shows up in the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew words like רִקְמָה (embroidered, multicolored cloth) and עָקֹד (streaked or spotted livestock). That literal coloring sense is vivid in the papyri, where an account of goats sorts them as black, red, and ποικίλαι (streaked).
prose.caution: With only nine New Testament occurrences and a meaning that ranges from concrete "many-colored" to abstract "manifold," the exact shade depends heavily on context.

prose.def: An interrogative word asking what kind, which, or what sort of thing or person is meant.

prose.def: To make war, fight in battle, or engage in armed conflict—and figuratively, to quarrel.
prose.article: πολεμέω means to make war or fight, whether in literal battle or figurative conflict. In the New Testament it appears only 7 times, six of them in Revelation describing warfare, while James 4:2 stretches it to private quarreling among people. It's a heavily used Septuagint word (165 times), almost always rendering Hebrew לָחַם ("to fight," 114 times); notably, the everyday Koine papyri show it construed with μετά ("war with")—as in a 5th-century document and a 6th-century inscription—so this construction in Revelation reflects ordinary Greek usage, not a Hebraism.
prose.caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences, the measured senses are thin, and most simply reflect the single core idea of waging war rendered with slightly different English wording.

issues: Sense label 2 reads 'course gain' — this appears to be a corrupted label (likely 'coarse gain' or an artifact) that is unexplained and misleading; BSB independently agrees 0% with it, suggesting it is not a real distinct sense but a contextual rendering artifact
The definition omits Abbott-Smith's primary sense 1, 'a providing' or 'furnishing,' which is the root semantic meaning and shapes how readers understand the theological contrast in 1 Ti 6:5-6

The two sense labels ('gain' vs. 'course gain') falsely imply two distinct semantic senses when both occurrences are in the same passage and reflect one lexical meaning shaped by immediate context, not two separate senses

receipts.how: Demonstrates the core sense 'means of gain' or 'source of profit' directly, where godliness is treated as a financial resource, supporting the definition's central claim.
Shows the same lemma one verse later; the identical lexical meaning ('means of gain') applies, exposing the 'course gain' label as a contextual artifact rather than a genuine second sense.

Abbott-Smith's sense 1 ('a providing') is the etymological base (from πορίζω, to procure), which the current definition bypasses entirely, narrowing the gloss to money specifically rather than procurement broadly.
